## Per-chapter highlights

### Chapter 1 — After the Death of Joshua: The Incomplete Conquest, Tribe by Tribe

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, prophetic-call

The book opens "after the death of Joshua." Israel asks who shall go up first; the LORD says Judah, who enlists Simeon and conducts a substantial southern campaign — Adonibezek, Jerusalem, Hebron, Othniel's capture of Debir (Josh 15:16-19 replayed) — until iron chariots block the valley. The chapter then extends Joshua's localized territorial-incomplete notations into a tribe-by-tribe pattern of failure across Benjamin, Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan.

### Chapter 2 — Bochim — Joshua's Death Recalled — the Cyclic-Pattern Installed

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, prophetic-call

An angel of the LORD comes up from Gilgal to Bochim and delivers a covenantal-lawsuit — Israel was to make no league with the inhabitants nor leave their altars, but did so; therefore the nations will remain as thorns in Israel's sides and their gods a snare. The people weep, sacrifice, and name the place "Weepers." The chapter then recalls Joshua's death and notes that another generation arose "which knew not the LORD." The cyclic-pattern programmatic statement at 2:11-23 installs the book's interpretive key: evil → oppression → cry → judge → rest → renewed evil.

### Chapter 3 — Othniel — Ehud — Shamgar: Three Judges, the First Cycles Executed

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

The remnant-nations the LORD left "to prove Israel" are named; the cyclic-pattern installed at Judges 2 begins its narrative execution. Othniel — Caleb's younger brother, the figure who closed Joshua's southern campaign and now closes the Joshua-to-Judges bridge — is the framework's compressed-clean first iteration (40 years of rest). Ehud the left-handed Benjamite delivers Israel from Eglon king of Moab via covert-assassination (80 years of rest, double Othniel's), and Shamgar's one-verse notation closes the chapter — six hundred Philistines slain with an ox goad.

### Chapter 4 — Deborah and Barak — Sisera at Kishon — Jael at the Tent

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

Israel returns to evil after Ehud's death; Jabin king of Canaan oppresses with nine hundred chariots of iron. Deborah the prophetess summons Barak from Kedesh-naphtali, conveys the LORD's battle-plan at the river Kishon, and — when Barak asks her to come — prophesies that the LORD will sell Sisera "into the hand of a woman." The battle goes Israel's way; Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael wife of Heber the Kenite, who drives a tent- peg through his temples while he sleeps — the prophecy's literal fulfillment and the iron-chariots framework's narrative-resolution at Kishon.

### Chapter 5 — The Song of Deborah: Hebrew Poetry's Witness to the Kishon Victory

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

Deborah and Barak sing the deliverance — preamble + Sinai- theophany imagery (5:1-5); pre-Deborah desolation and her rise as "a mother in Israel" (5:6-8); the tribal participation roll- call naming who came and who did not (5:9-18); the cosmic- battle at Megiddo with the stars in their courses fighting against Sisera and the river of Kishon sweeping them away (5:19-22); the curse of Meroz + the Jael celebration as the song's centerpiece (5:23-27); the mother of Sisera at the window waiting in vain + the closing curse-and-blessing benediction (5:28-31).

### Chapter 6 — Gideon Called: The Angel of the LORD Under the Oak at Ophrah

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

The Midianites and Amalekites oppress Israel seven years; an unnamed prophet recaps the Exodus and Israel's failure. The angel of the LORD sits under the oak at Ophrah while Gideon threshes hidden wheat, commissions him with "Go in this thy might," and grants a fire-from-the-rock sign. Gideon throws down his father's Baal-altar (earning the name Jerubbaal), the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him, and the fleece sign sequence twice confirms the promise to save Israel by his hand.

### Chapter 7 — The Three Hundred — the Midianite Dream — 'The Sword of the LORD, and of Gideon'

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

The LORD reduces Gideon's army from twenty-two thousand to three hundred — "lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me" — first by sending the fearful home, then by the water-drinking test. A Midianite dream of a barley-cake overturning a tent confirms the deliverance; three companies of a hundred blow trumpets, break pitchers, raise lamps, and cry "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon," and the LORD sets every man's sword against his fellow. Naphtali, Asher, Manasseh, and Ephraim pursue; the princes Oreb and Zeeb are captured and slain.

### Chapter 8 — Gideon's Pursuit, Anti-Monarchy Refusal, and Ephod Compromise

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

Gideon deflects Ephraim's complaint with diplomatic humility, then pursues Zebah and Zalmunna across the Jordan; Succoth and Penuel refuse bread to his weary three hundred and receive judgment after the kings are taken. Israel offers Gideon kingship; he refuses — "the LORD shall rule over you" — yet asks for the golden earrings of the spoil, makes an ephod at Ophrah, and "all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house." The land has rest forty years; Gideon dies; Israel returns to Baalim and Baalberith.

### Chapter 9 — Abimelech at Shechem — Jotham's Parable — the Curse Fulfilled

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, prophetic-call

Abimelech, Gideon's son by the Shechem concubine, takes seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baalberith and slays his seventy brothers on one stone — all but Jotham, who hides. From Mount Gerizim Jotham delivers the parable of the trees and pronounces a conditional curse. After three years God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem; Gaal's revolt fails, Abimelech burns Shechem and the tower of Shechem, and dies at Thebez when a woman drops a millstone on his head — the closure- formula names the rendering and Jotham's curse fulfilled.

### Chapter 10 — Tola and Jair; the LORD's 'I Will Deliver You No More' + Gilead's Question

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, prophetic-call

Tola the Issacharite judges Israel twenty-three years and Jair the Gileadite twenty-two more (with thirty sons on thirty asses in thirty cities). Israel then serves seven foreign gods and is sold into the hands of the Philistines and Ammon; when Israel cries, the LORD lists seven prior deliverances and answers "Go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen... I will deliver you no more." Israel puts away the strange gods, "his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel," and the princes of Gilead at Mizpeh ask who will lead against Ammon — and he shall be their head.

### Chapter 11 — Jephthah: From Thrust-Out Son to Gileadite Head — the Vow and the Daughter

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

Jephthah the Gileadite — son of a harlot, thrust out by his half- brothers — is fetched from exile by the elders of Gilead and made head at Mizpeh; he answers Ammon's territorial claim with a historical-recap of Israel's wilderness journey and the Amorite conquest. The Spirit of the LORD comes upon him, and he vows that whatsoever comes forth of his house to meet him on his return shall be the LORD's. Ammon is delivered; his only child, his daughter, comes out with timbrels — and after two months bewailing her virginity in the mountains, "her father... did with her according to his vow."

### Chapter 12 — The Shibboleth at Jordan; Ibzan, Elon, Abdon Close the Jephthah Block

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, prophetic-call

Ephraim confronts Jephthah for not being called against Ammon — the complaint Gideon defused at Judg 8:1-3, here not defused; Jephthah gathers Gilead, the Gileadites take the Jordan fords, and the Shibboleth / Sibboleth pronunciation-test identifies and slays forty-two thousand Ephraimites. Jephthah dies after six years. Ibzan of Bethlehem judges seven years; Elon the Zebulonite ten years; Abdon the Pirathonite eight years — three minor judges bracket the cycle's close.

### Chapter 13 — The Angel at Zorah: Samson Announced — the Theophany-Trajectory Completes

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, deliverance

Israel is delivered into the hand of the Philistines forty years. The angel of the LORD appears to Manoah's barren wife at Zorah, announcing a son who shall be a Nazarite from the womb and begin to deliver Israel; the angel returns at Manoah's prayer, refuses to give his name ("seeing it is secret"), and ascends in the flame of the kid-offering on the rock. The Spirit of the LORD begins to move Samson "in the camp of Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol" — the fourth and final instance of the OT theophany-commissioning trajectory.

### Chapter 14 — The Timnathite Wife, the Lion, and the Riddle

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

Samson sees a Philistine woman at Timnath and demands his parents get her — the narrator notes "it was of the LORD, that he sought an occasion against the Philistines." The Spirit comes mightily on him and he rends a lion; later he eats honey from the carcass (Nazirite corpse-contact). At the seven-day wedding feast he puts forth a riddle; the companions threaten his wife to extract the answer; the Spirit comes again and he slays thirty men at Ashkelon for the garments, and his wife is given to his companion.

### Chapter 15 — Samson's Vengeance: The Foxes, the Jawbone, the Twenty Years

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

Samson returns with a kid; his wife has been given to his companion. He catches three hundred foxes, ties firebrands to their tails, and burns the Philistine corn, vineyards, and olives; the Philistines retaliate by burning the wife and her father. Three thousand men of Judah bind Samson and deliver him at Lehi; the Spirit of the LORD comes mightily on him, the cords burn off, with a new jawbone of an ass he slays a thousand men; the LORD cleaves a hollow in the jaw for water; Samson judges Israel twenty years.

### Chapter 16 — Delilah, the Seven Locks, and the Pillars of Dagon's House

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, deliverance, prophetic-call

Samson carries off the gates of Gaza, then loves Delilah in the valley of Sorek; the Philistine lords offer eleven hundred pieces of silver each, and after three failed tests Samson tells her his Nazirite hair is the secret. She has the seven locks shaved — "he wist not that the LORD was departed from him"; the Philistines put out his eyes and set him grinding at Gaza, but his hair grows again. At a sacrifice to Dagon, Samson prays "remember me... strengthen me, only this once," pushes down the two middle pillars, and the dead at his death are more than they which he slew in his life.

### Chapter 17 — Micah's Graven Image and the Levite-Priest — 'No King in Israel'

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, judgment, prophetic-call

Micah of mount Ephraim restores eleven hundred shekels of silver to his mother, who dedicates two hundred to make a graven image and molten image installed in his "house of gods" with an ephod and teraphim; Micah consecrates his son priest, and later hires a young Levite from Bethlehem-judah for ten shekels a year. The chapter installs the appendix-narratives' interpretive-key formula at 17:6 — "In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes."
